name: Security and Risk Management

topics.d: The CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) is the foundational model for information security, extended by IAAA (Identification, Authentication, Authorization, Auditing/Accountability).

topics.t: Security Governance: Policies, Frameworks, and Roles
topics.d: Security governance establishes the organizational structure, roles, and documentation hierarchy (Policy > Standards > Baselines > Guidelines > Procedures) guided by frameworks like COBIT, COSO, and ITIL.
Risk management involves identifying, analyzing (quantitatively and qualitatively), and treating risks using formulas (SLE, ALE, CBA) and treatment options: Mitigate, Accept, Avoid, Transfer (MAAT).

topics.t: Threat Modeling: STRIDE, DREAD, and PASTA
topics.d: Threat modeling identifies and prioritizes threats using structured methodologies: STRIDE (classification by Microsoft), DREAD (risk rating), and PASTA (7-stage risk-centric process).

topics.t: Business Continuity Planning (BCP) and Disaster Recovery
topics.d: BCP ensures critical business functions continue during and after a disaster. The BIA identifies critical functions and recovery metrics (MTD, RTO, RPO). Human safety is always the top priority.
Security professionals must understand categories of law (Criminal, Civil, Administrative), key legislation, data classification systems, and the ISC2 Code of Ethics with its four mandatory canons.

SCRM addresses risks from third-party vendors, suppliers, and service providers throughout the entire supply chain lifecycle using frameworks like NIST SP 800-161 and controls such as SLAs, audits, and hardware/software verification.
Personnel security controls span the entire employment lifecycle — from background checks and NDAs during hiring to exit interviews and immediate access revocation during termination.

A comprehensive security program includes three levels: Awareness (all employees, behavioral), Training (role-specific technical skills), and Education (in-depth understanding for security professionals).

topics.t: Intellectual Property: Copyright, Patent, Trademark, Trade Secret
topics.d: Four types of intellectual property protection exist: Copyright (creative works, automatic, life+70 years), Patent (inventions, 20 years), Trademark (brand identity, renewable indefinitely), and Trade Secret (proprietary processes, no expiration if kept secret).

topics.t: Privacy Legislation: GDPR, HIPAA, GLBA, and Global Privacy Laws
topics.d: Major privacy laws define how personal data must be collected, processed, stored, and destroyed. GDPR (EU), HIPAA (US healthcare), GLBA (US finance), and various national laws each have distinct requirements and penalties.

topics.t: Risk Frameworks: NIST RMF, ISO 31000, and COSO ERM
topics.d: Risk management frameworks provide structured approaches. NIST RMF (6 steps for federal systems), ISO 31000 (universal risk management principles), and COSO ERM (enterprise risk management integrated with strategy).

topics.t: Security Control Categories, Types, and Functions
topics.d: Controls are categorized by implementation (Technical/Administrative/Physical) and by function (Preventive, Detective, Corrective, Deterrent, Compensating, Recovery, Directive). Understanding the matrix is essential for CISSP.
Compliance ensures adherence to laws, regulations, and standards. Internal/external audits verify compliance. Key frameworks include PCI-DSS, SOX, FISMA, and industry-specific regulations.

topics.t: Security Control Frameworks: NIST SP 800-53 and ISO 27001
topics.d: NIST SP 800-53 provides a catalog of security and privacy controls organized by family. ISO 27001 defines ISMS requirements. Together they form the basis for implementing comprehensive security programs.

Security must be integrated into M&A activities. Due diligence includes security assessments of target companies. Data handling, system integration, and access control changes present significant risks during organizational transitions.

topics.t: Import/Export Controls and Transborder Data Flow
topics.d: Cryptographic products and technologies are subject to export controls (EAR, ITAR, Wassenaar Arrangement). Cross-border data transfers must comply with privacy laws and international agreements.

Four types of evidence: Real (physical objects), Documentary (documents/logs), Testimonial (witness statements), and Demonstrative (models/simulations). Evidence must be relevant, reliable, and legally obtained.

Key US computer crime laws include CFAA, ECPA, and the Identity Theft Enforcement Act. International frameworks include the Budapest Convention. Understanding jurisdiction and evidence collection is critical.
Beyond the ISC2 Code of Ethics, organizations must establish ethical frameworks including codes of conduct, ethics committees, whistleblower protections, and conflict of interest policies.

Change management ensures modifications to systems follow a controlled process: request, review, approve, implement, verify, document. Configuration management maintains known-good system states through baselines and inventories.

Advanced quantitative techniques include Monte Carlo simulation, decision tree analysis, sensitivity analysis, and Bayesian analysis. These methods provide more nuanced risk assessments beyond basic SLE/ALE calculations.

topics.t: Types of Law: Criminal, Civil, Administrative, and Common vs. Civil Law Systems
topics.d: Understanding the distinctions between criminal law (imprisonment), civil/tort law (monetary damages), and administrative/regulatory law (government regulations), plus the difference between common law and civil law legal systems.

Organizations need multiple policy types: Organizational (strategic), Issue-specific (topic-focused like AUP), and System-specific (platform-focused). Policies must be management-approved, enforceable, and regularly reviewed.
Qualitative risk analysis uses subjective ratings (High/Medium/Low) through techniques like Delphi method, brainstorming, interviews, and risk matrices. Faster than quantitative but less precise.

The BIA is the most critical phase of BCP. It identifies critical business functions, determines maximum tolerable downtime (MTD), and establishes recovery priorities. BIA drives all subsequent BCP/DR decisions.

topics.t: Disaster Recovery Site Types and Strategies
topics.d: DR site types range from hot (immediate failover) to cold (weeks to activate). Additional options include mobile sites, cloud DR, and reciprocal agreements. Site selection depends on RTO, cost, and risk tolerance.

topics.t: Third-Party Risk Management and Vendor Assessment
topics.d: Organizations must assess and manage risks from third-party relationships through due diligence, contractual controls, ongoing monitoring, and exit strategies. SOC reports, right-to-audit, and SLAs are key tools.

topics.t: Privacy Principles and Data Protection Concepts
topics.d: Privacy principles including purpose limitation, data minimization, consent, transparency, and individual rights form the foundation of modern privacy law. The OECD Guidelines and GAPP provide universal frameworks.

Effective security governance requires clear organizational structures: Board of Directors (oversight), CEO (ultimate accountability), CISO (security strategy), security committee (cross-functional coordination), and defined roles at every level.

Below policies in the hierarchy: Standards (mandatory specific requirements), Baselines (minimum security configurations), Guidelines (optional recommendations), and Procedures (step-by-step instructions). Each serves a distinct purpose.

Threat intelligence involves collecting, analyzing, and sharing information about current and emerging threats. Sources include OSINT, ISACs, STIX/TAXII, and commercial feeds. Intelligence must be timely, relevant, and actionable.

topics.t: Business Continuity Plan Testing and Maintenance
topics.d: BCP/DR plans must be regularly tested using increasingly disruptive methods: checklist review, tabletop exercise, walkthrough, simulation, parallel test, and full interruption test. Plans also require regular maintenance and updates.

Risk appetite is the level of risk an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of objectives. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around appetite. Risk capacity is the maximum risk an organization can absorb.
Security planning operates at three horizons: Strategic (3-5 years), Tactical (6-12 months), and Operational (days to weeks). Each level translates security vision into actionable implementation.

Data breach notification laws require organizations to notify affected individuals, regulators, and sometimes media within specified timeframes. Requirements vary by jurisdiction: GDPR (72 hours), HIPAA (60 days), US state laws (varies).

topics.t: Defense in Depth and Layered Security
topics.d: Defense in depth uses multiple layers of security controls so that if one layer fails, others continue to protect. Layers span physical, technical, and administrative controls across the entire environment.
The formal process of evaluating security controls and granting authorization to operate (ATO). Replaces the older Certification and Accreditation (C&A) terminology. Follows NIST SP 800-37 RMF.

Security professionals must understand how contracts, laws, and regulations create binding obligations. Key concepts include liability, due care, negligence, contractual security requirements, and regulatory penalties.

topics.t: Continuous Improvement and Security Program Maturity
topics.d: Security programs must continuously improve using maturity models (CMM/CMMI), metrics, KPIs, and regular assessments. The goal is progressing from ad-hoc to optimized security operations.

After identifying risks, organizations must select appropriate responses and controls. The cost of a control should never exceed the value of the asset it protects. Control selection considers effectiveness, cost, operational impact, and regulatory requirements.

Software licensing defines legal usage rights. Types include proprietary, open source (GPL, MIT, Apache, BSD), per-seat, site, enterprise, and SaaS subscriptions. Piracy and non-compliance carry legal and security risks.

topics.t: Investigations: Administrative, Civil, Criminal, and Regulatory
topics.d: Different investigation types have different objectives, authorities, evidence standards, and outcomes. Understanding these distinctions is critical for incident response and forensic decisions.

topics.t: Separation of Duties, Least Privilege, and Need-to-Know
topics.d: Three foundational access control principles: Separation of Duties (SoD) prevents fraud by requiring multiple people. Least Privilege grants minimum necessary access. Need-to-Know restricts access even within clearance level.
Comparing NIST CSF, ISO 27001/27002, COBIT, CIS Controls, and NIST SP 800-53 for organizational security governance and control selection.

topics.t: Ethics, Professional Conduct, and Legal Compliance
topics.d: ISC2 Code of Ethics, professional ethical obligations, conflicts of interest, whistleblowing, and the intersection of ethics with legal compliance.
Managing security risks throughout the supply chain including vendor assessment, third-party risk, SLA requirements, and supply chain attack prevention.
Conducting BIA including identifying critical business functions, determining MTD/RTO/RPO, resource dependencies, and impact categories.
Systematic approaches to identifying and prioritizing threats including STRIDE, PASTA, DREAD, OCTAVE, VAST, and attack trees.

topics.t: Security Awareness, Education, and Training Programs
topics.d: Building effective security awareness programs including program design, content development, delivery methods, measurement, and continuous improvement.
Developing incident response plans, establishing incident classification, and integrating with business continuity for comprehensive organizational resilience.
Understanding the legal and regulatory landscape affecting information security including jurisdictional issues, data breach laws, and compliance requirements.
Comparing risk assessment approaches including NIST, ISO, FAIR, OCTAVE, and integrating risk management into organizational decision-making.
Organizational structures for security governance including CISO reporting, security committees, roles and responsibilities, and executive accountability.
Ensuring critical government and organizational functions continue during disruptions including succession planning, alternate sites, and devolution.

topics.t: Maximum Tolerable Downtime and Recovery Metrics Deep Dive
topics.d: MTD, RTO, RPO, WRT, and MTPD form a hierarchy of recovery metrics that drive BCP strategy. Understanding the relationships between these metrics is essential for the exam.
The ISC2 Code of Ethics has a preamble and four mandatory canons prioritized in order. Canon 1 (protect society) always takes precedence. Violations can result in revocation of certification.

Determining asset value is foundational to risk analysis. Methods include replacement cost, revenue generation, book value, and impact analysis. Tangible and intangible assets require different approaches.

topics.t: Security Awareness Program Design and Measurement
topics.d: Effective security awareness programs target all employees with role-appropriate content, use varied delivery methods, and measure effectiveness through metrics like phishing click rates and incident reporting.

Key security roles include the Board of Directors (ultimate governance), CEO (overall responsibility), CISO (security program), Data Owner (classification), Data Custodian (day-to-day), and Data Processor (handles data for controller).
Understanding the three branches of law, burden of proof standards, and how they apply to information security incidents is critical for CISSP.

topics.t: Privacy Principles: OECD, GAPP, and Fair Information Practices
topics.d: Foundational privacy frameworks including the OECD Privacy Guidelines (8 principles), GAPP (10 principles), and FIPs establish the basis for most privacy legislation worldwide.

topics.t: Export Controls: EAR, ITAR, and Wassenaar Arrangement
topics.d: Encryption technology is subject to export controls. EAR covers commercial/dual-use items, ITAR covers military/defense items, and the Wassenaar Arrangement coordinates export controls internationally.

GRC integrates governance (direction and oversight), risk management (identifying and treating threats), and compliance (meeting requirements) into a unified program that aligns security with business objectives.

Control baselines provide a starting set of security controls based on system categorization. Tailoring adjusts these baselines to the specific environment through scoping, compensating controls, and supplementation.

topics.t: Cyber Kill Chain and Attack Frameworks
topics.d: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, MITRE ATT&CK, and Diamond Model provide complementary frameworks for understanding, detecting, and disrupting adversary operations.

Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Attack types include phishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating, and quid pro quo. Defense relies on awareness training and verification procedures.

topics.t: Computer Crime Laws: CFAA, ECPA, and International Frameworks
topics.d: Key cybercrime laws include CFAA (unauthorized access), ECPA (electronic communications privacy), and the Council of Europe Convention on Cybercrime. Understanding jurisdiction and evidence admissibility is essential.

Different jurisdictions have varying breach notification requirements. GDPR requires 72-hour authority notification, HIPAA requires 60-day individual notification, and US state laws vary by jurisdiction.

topics.t: Risk Appetite Frameworks and Risk Register
topics.d: Risk appetite defines how much risk an organization is willing to accept to achieve objectives. Risk registers document identified risks, their assessment, treatment plans, and ownership.

Cyber insurance transfers financial risk of security incidents to an insurer. Coverage types include first-party (own losses) and third-party (liability). Understanding policy exclusions and coverage limits is critical.

topics.t: Regulatory Frameworks: SOX, PCI DSS, FISMA
topics.d: SOX protects investors through financial reporting controls, PCI DSS secures payment card data, and FISMA mandates security for federal information systems. Each has specific compliance requirements.
Digital evidence must be collected, preserved, and presented following legal standards. Key concepts include the Best Evidence Rule, chain of custody, hearsay, and the five types of evidence.

Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) per NIST SP 800-137 maintains ongoing awareness of security posture through automated data feeds, metrics, and dashboards replacing point-in-time assessments.

topics.t: Organizational Security Models: NIST CSF and ISO 27001
topics.d: NIST CSF provides a risk-based framework with five core functions. ISO 27001 is a certifiable ISMS standard. Understanding both frameworks, their differences, and when to use each is essential.

topics.t: NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF) Deep Dive
topics.d: The NIST RMF provides a structured process for managing security and privacy risk. Six steps: Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, and Monitor. Required for US federal systems.
Understanding legal liability concepts including negligence, downstream liability, vicarious liability, and safe harbor provisions is critical for security managers making risk decisions.

Personnel security spans the entire employment lifecycle: pre-employment screening, onboarding, ongoing monitoring, role changes, and termination. Each phase has specific security controls to mitigate insider threat risk.

Maturity models measure how well an organization's security program is developed and operating. CMM, CMMI, and the NIST CSF implementation tiers help organizations assess their current state and plan improvements.

PII includes any information that can identify a specific individual. Direct identifiers (SSN, name) and quasi-identifiers (ZIP + age + gender) both create risk. Protection strategies must address both types.

Measuring security program effectiveness requires meaningful metrics aligned with business objectives. Metrics should demonstrate risk reduction, compliance status, and operational efficiency to justify security investment.

Key US compliance frameworks affect information security: HIPAA protects health information, SOX protects financial integrity, and GLBA protects financial consumer data. Each has specific security requirements.

Security must be integrated into the procurement process. Vendor risk assessment evaluates the security posture of potential suppliers before contracts are signed. Assessment depth should match the risk level.

Intellectual property (IP) includes trade secrets, patents, copyrights, and trademarks. Each has different legal protections, durations, and requirements. Understanding IP types is essential for security professionals.

Multiple governance frameworks guide security program management: COBIT, ITIL, NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and TOGAF. Understanding their focus, strengths, and relationships helps organizations choose the right framework.

topics.t: Ethics and Professional Conduct in Security
topics.d: Security professionals face ethical dilemmas involving privacy, disclosure, conflicts of interest, and professional responsibility. ISC2 Code of Ethics, organizational codes, and RFC 1087 provide guidance.
Supply chain risk management (SCRM) addresses security risks introduced by vendors, suppliers, and service providers throughout the product and service lifecycle.

Security awareness programs change user behavior to reduce human-factor security risks. Effective programs combine education (why), training (how), and awareness (ongoing reinforcement) with metrics to measure effectiveness.

The BIA identifies critical business functions and the impact of their disruption. It determines MTD, RTO, RPO, and resource requirements for each function. The BIA is the foundation of BCP/DR planning.

name: Asset Security

topics.t: Data Classification and Sensitive Data Types
topics.d: Data must be classified by sensitivity. Government: Top Secret > Secret > Confidential > Unclassified. Private sector: Confidential > Private > Sensitive > Public. Key data types include PII, PHI, and proprietary data.
Data Owner (classifies, ultimately responsible), Data Custodian (day-to-day protection), Data Controller (determines processing purpose), Data Processor (processes on behalf of controller).
Data at rest (AES-256), in motion (TLS/VPN), and in use (memory isolation). Tokenization replaces data with tokens that have no mathematical relationship to the original.
Destruction hierarchy: Erasing < Clearing < Purging < Sanitization < Destruction. Data remanence is residual data after deletion. Degaussing only works on magnetic media (NOT SSDs).
Pseudonymization (replaceable identifiers, still personal data), anonymization (permanent, no longer personal data), data masking, and the full data lifecycle from creation through destruction.

topics.t: Data Security Controls and Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
topics.d: DLP systems detect and prevent unauthorized data exfiltration across three deployment points: network (data in motion), endpoint (data in use), and storage (data at rest). Combined with data rights management (DRM/IRM) and database activity monitoring (DAM).

topics.t: Data Retention Policies and Record Management
topics.d: Data retention policies define how long data must be kept and when it must be destroyed. Requirements come from regulations (SOX 7 years, HIPAA 6 years), business needs, and legal holds that override normal destruction schedules.

All organizational assets must be inventoried and classified. Asset types include hardware, software, data, and personnel. Classification drives the security controls applied. Asset management is continuous throughout the asset lifecycle.

Physical and digital media must be handled according to classification level. Controls include marking/labeling, secure storage, controlled transport, and proper sanitization before reuse or disposal.

Anonymization irreversibly removes PII (no longer personal data under GDPR). De-identification uses techniques like k-anonymity, l-diversity, and t-closeness. Pseudonymization is reversible and data remains personal data under GDPR.

topics.t: Cloud Data Security and Shared Responsibility
topics.d: Cloud computing shifts data security responsibilities between provider and customer based on service model. IaaS gives customers most control, SaaS gives least. The shared responsibility model defines who secures what.

Data ownership defines who has ultimate responsibility for data throughout its lifecycle. Roles include Data Owner, Data Steward, Data Controller, and Data Processor, each with distinct responsibilities and accountability levels.
ILM manages data from creation through disposal across six phases: Create, Store, Use, Share, Archive, and Destroy. Each phase requires appropriate security controls based on classification.

topics.t: Encryption for Data Protection: Methods and Key Management
topics.d: Data protection relies on encryption: symmetric (AES — fast, bulk data), asymmetric (RSA/ECC — key exchange, digital signatures), and hybrid approaches. Key management is critical — poor key management undermines all encryption.

topics.t: Data Sovereignty and Cross-Border Data Transfer
topics.d: Data sovereignty requires that data is subject to the laws of the country where it resides. Cross-border transfers require legal mechanisms (GDPR SCCs, BCRs, adequacy decisions). Cloud computing complicates sovereignty.

NIST 800-88 Rev. 1 defines three sanitization levels: Clear (overwrite), Purge (make unrecoverable), and Destroy (physical destruction). The appropriate level depends on security categorization and whether media will be reused.

Data security requirements differ across environments: on-premises (full control), cloud (shared responsibility), mobile (BYOD/MDM), IoT (limited compute), and legacy systems (outdated controls). Each requires tailored approaches.

Scoping identifies which security controls apply to a system. Tailoring modifies selected controls to fit the organizational context. Together they ensure controls are appropriate — not excessive or insufficient.

topics.t: Digital Rights Management (DRM) and Information Rights Management (IRM)
topics.d: DRM protects digital content (music, video, software) from unauthorized use. IRM extends this concept to business documents with persistent protection that travels with the data regardless of location.

Security baselines define minimum acceptable configurations. Key baselines include CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, and vendor-specific guides. Baselines must be applied, monitored, and updated as threats evolve.

topics.t: Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) and Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
topics.d: PIAs and DPIAs systematically identify and mitigate privacy risks before systems go live. GDPR mandates DPIAs for high-risk processing. Both assess necessity, proportionality, and risks to individuals.

Secure provisioning ensures resources (hardware, software, cloud, personnel) are deployed with appropriate security controls from the start. It includes procurement security, secure configuration, and access control setup.

All data and media must be marked with classification levels. Handling procedures define how data at each level may be stored, transmitted, processed, and destroyed. Proper labeling prevents accidental disclosure.
DLP technologies, deployment modes, policy configuration, and integration with data classification for preventing unauthorized data exposure.
Organizational structures for data management including data governance frameworks, data quality, metadata management, and data stewardship roles.

topics.t: Cloud Data Security and Shared Responsibility
topics.d: Protecting data in cloud environments including encryption strategies, key management, data residency, and cloud-specific data security controls.

topics.t: Privacy Impact Assessments and Data Protection
topics.d: Conducting PIAs/DPIAs, implementing privacy-enhancing technologies, and applying data protection principles including purpose limitation and data minimization.

topics.t: Information Rights Management (IRM) and Digital Rights Management (DRM)
topics.d: Technologies for persistent data protection including document rights management, usage controls, watermarking, and enterprise IRM deployment.
Methods for securely destroying data across different media types including magnetic, solid-state, optical, and cloud environments.
Protecting data in all three states: at rest, in transit, and in use, with appropriate encryption and access control for each state.

Proper data ownership assigns clear accountability for data classification, protection, and lifecycle management. Understanding the distinction between owner, custodian, steward, processor, and controller is heavily tested.

Organizations must retain data for legally mandated periods while disposing of it when retention expires. Over-retention increases risk; under-retention violates compliance. Legal holds override all retention schedules.

Three key data protection techniques with different characteristics: encryption (reversible with key), tokenization (random substitution with vault), and masking (irreversible transformation). Each suits different use cases.

Cloud computing introduces unique data security challenges. The shared responsibility model defines who secures what. Customer ALWAYS owns data security regardless of cloud service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).

A formal data classification process includes identifying data, determining classification criteria, assigning labels, implementing controls, and periodically reviewing classifications. Both over- and under-classification waste resources or create risk.

Object reuse occurs when storage media is reassigned to a new user/process without proper sanitization. Data remanence is residual data remaining after deletion. Both create risks of unauthorized information disclosure.

Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it physically resides. Data residency requires data to remain within specific geographic boundaries. Cloud computing makes both increasingly complex.

Advanced anonymization techniques prevent re-identification of individuals in datasets. Each technique addresses specific weaknesses in simpler approaches, from k-anonymity through l-diversity to t-closeness.
A CASB sits between cloud users and cloud services to enforce security policies, provide visibility into shadow IT, protect data, and ensure compliance across cloud environments.
Data passes through distinct lifecycle phases: Create, Store, Use, Share, Archive, and Destroy. Each phase requires appropriate security controls to protect data throughout its existence.

topics.t: European Data Protection: GDPR Deep Dive
topics.d: GDPR is the most comprehensive privacy regulation globally. Key concepts include lawful bases for processing, data subject rights, DPO requirements, 72-hour breach notification, and extraterritorial scope.
Proper data handling procedures ensure information is protected throughout its lifecycle. Media management covers labeling, storage, transportation, and sanitization of physical and electronic media.

DLP systems detect and prevent unauthorized data exfiltration. Three deployment points protect data at rest, in motion, and in use. Detection methods include exact matching, regex, fingerprinting, and machine learning.

topics.t: Sensitive Data Types and Regulatory Mapping
topics.d: Different types of sensitive data (PII, PHI, PCI, IP) are protected by different regulations. Understanding which regulations apply to which data types drives control selection and compliance strategy.

topics.t: Cloud Security Alliance and CSA STAR
topics.d: The Cloud Security Alliance provides the Cloud Controls Matrix and STAR registry for evaluating cloud provider security. Understanding CCM, CAIQ, and STAR certification levels helps with cloud vendor assessment.

Records management ensures organizational records are created, maintained, and disposed of in accordance with legal, regulatory, and business requirements. Legal holds override all retention schedules when litigation is anticipated.

Assets must be provisioned with security from the start and decommissioned with proper data sanitization. The asset lifecycle requires security at acquisition, deployment, operation, maintenance, and disposal.

Comparing encryption, tokenization, masking, hashing, obfuscation, and anonymization helps select the right data protection method for each use case. Each technique has different reversibility, performance, and compliance characteristics.

topics.t: Scoping and Tailoring Data Protection Controls
topics.d: Scoping determines which security controls apply to a specific system based on the data it processes. Tailoring adjusts baseline controls to meet specific organizational requirements and risk tolerance.
Data integrity ensures information is accurate, complete, consistent, and trustworthy throughout its lifecycle. Controls include input validation, referential integrity, checksums, and audit trails.
Secure data sharing enables collaboration while maintaining confidentiality and compliance. Technologies include DRM, IRM, secure file sharing, data rooms, and privacy-preserving techniques.

topics.t: Physical Asset Security and Facility Protection
topics.d: Physical asset security protects hardware, media, and facilities from theft, damage, and unauthorized access. It includes access controls, environmental controls, and asset tracking throughout the lifecycle.
Data backup strategies protect against data loss from hardware failure, human error, malware, and disasters. The 3-2-1 rule, backup types, and recovery objectives guide backup program design.

topics.t: Third-Party and Cloud Data Processing Agreements
topics.d: When third parties process your data, proper agreements are essential. Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) under GDPR, Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) under HIPAA, and service level agreements define responsibilities and protections.

name: Security Architecture and Engineering

topics.d: Cryptography achieves four goals: Privacy (confidentiality), Authentication, Integrity, Non-Repudiation. Key space = 2^n. Kerckhoffs' Principle: security depends on key secrecy, not algorithm secrecy.

Symmetric uses one shared key (AES, 3DES) — fast but key distribution problem. Asymmetric uses key pairs (RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman) — scalable but slow. Hybrid systems combine both. Digital signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.

Bell-LaPadula enforces confidentiality (no read up, no write down). Biba enforces integrity (no read down, no write up). Clark-Wilson uses well-formed transactions and separation of duties for commercial integrity.

topics.t: Secure Design Principles and Zero Trust
topics.d: Defense in depth layers multiple controls. Zero trust assumes breach and verifies continuously. Fail-secure denies access on failure. Fail-open allows access. Least privilege, complete mediation, economy of mechanism, and separation of duties are foundational principles.

Hashing creates fixed-length digests for integrity (SHA-256, SHA-3). PKI uses Certificate Authorities to bind public keys to identities. Certificate lifecycle includes issuance, renewal, and revocation (CRL, OCSP). HMAC combines hashing with a secret key for authentication.

Physical security uses layered perimeters: fencing, lighting, CCTV, guards. Mantrap/vestibule prevents tailgating. Server room controls: positive pressurization, FM-200 suppression, raised floors. HVAC maintains temperature/humidity. Power: UPS for short-term, generators for long-term.

topics.t: Cryptographic Key Management and Key Lifecycle
topics.d: Cryptographic key management covers the entire key lifecycle — generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation, and destruction — along with key escrow, key recovery, and split knowledge/dual control principles.

topics.t: Elliptic Curve Cryptography and Modern Algorithms
topics.d: ECC provides equivalent security to RSA with much smaller key sizes (256-bit ECC equals 3072-bit RSA). Understanding algorithm selection, key sizes, and the impact of quantum computing on current cryptographic systems.

topics.t: Security Evaluation Models: Common Criteria and TCSEC
topics.d: TCSEC (Orange Book) rated systems A1-D. Common Criteria (ISO 15408) replaced it with Evaluation Assurance Levels (EAL1-7). Protection Profiles define requirements; Security Targets describe implementation.

Hardware security includes TPM (key storage, measured boot), HSM (cryptographic operations), Secure Boot (firmware integrity), and hardware roots of trust. These form the foundation for system integrity.

topics.t: State Machine Model and Information Flow Model
topics.d: The state machine model ensures a system is secure in every possible state. The information flow model tracks how data moves between subjects and objects, preventing unauthorized information flows (covert channels).

topics.t: Processor Security: Protection Rings and Memory Protection
topics.d: Processor protection rings (0-3) enforce privilege separation. Ring 0 = kernel (most privileged), Ring 3 = user applications (least privileged). Memory protection mechanisms prevent processes from accessing each other's memory space.

Virtualization introduces security concerns: VM escape (breaking out of VM to hypervisor), VM sprawl (unmanaged VMs), inter-VM attacks, and hypervisor vulnerabilities. Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors are more secure than Type 2 (hosted).

Cryptanalytic attacks attempt to break encryption: Brute Force (try all keys), Known Plaintext (have some plaintext-ciphertext pairs), Chosen Plaintext (choose plaintexts to encrypt), Ciphertext-Only (only ciphertext available), Birthday Attack (collision finding), Side-Channel (physical leakage).

topics.t: PKI: Certificate Authorities, Certificate Lifecycle, and Trust Models
topics.d: Public Key Infrastructure binds identities to public keys through Certificate Authorities (CAs). Certificate lifecycle includes issuance, renewal, suspension, and revocation. Trust models: hierarchical, bridge, mesh, and web of trust.

Hash functions produce fixed-size digests: MD5 (128-bit, broken), SHA-1 (160-bit, broken), SHA-256/SHA-3 (secure). HMAC combines hashing with a secret key for authentication. Digital signatures use hashing with asymmetric encryption for non-repudiation.

Block ciphers operate in different modes: ECB (insecure, patterns preserved), CBC (XOR with previous block), CTR (counter mode, parallelizable), GCM (authenticated encryption). Mode selection affects security, performance, and functionality.

topics.t: Physical Security: Perimeter, Environmental, and Fire Controls
topics.d: Physical security uses layered controls: perimeter (fences, gates, lighting), building (locks, mantraps, CCTV), environmental (HVAC, humidity), and fire suppression (wet pipe, dry pipe, FM-200, Halon alternatives).

topics.t: Secure Architecture Patterns: SOA, Microservices, and Serverless
topics.d: Modern architecture patterns introduce security considerations. Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) uses web services. Microservices decompose into small, independent services. Serverless shifts responsibility to the cloud provider. Each pattern has unique attack surfaces.

Key management is more important than algorithm choice. The lifecycle includes generation (secure random), distribution (secure channel), storage (HSM/vault), use (proper algorithm/mode), rotation, archival, and destruction.

Secure facility design addresses site selection (natural hazards, proximity to threats), construction materials, utility systems (power, water, HVAC), and specialized areas (server rooms, Faraday cages, SCIFs).

IoT and embedded systems present unique security challenges: limited computing power, long lifecycles, default credentials, lack of patching capability, and massive scale. Security requires network isolation, firmware integrity, and lifecycle management.
Formal security models including lattice-based access control, non-interference models, and composition theories for system security evaluation.
Security considerations for cloud computing models including IaaS, PaaS, SaaS shared responsibility, cloud security controls, and cloud-native security tools.
Managing the lifecycle of cryptographic systems including algorithm selection, key length requirements, crypto agility, and transitioning from deprecated algorithms.
Attacks exploiting physical characteristics of cryptographic implementations including timing, power analysis, electromagnetic emanation, and cache-based attacks.
The reference monitor concept, security kernel implementation, Trusted Computing Base, and formal verification of security properties.

topics.t: Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption Deep Dive
topics.d: Detailed comparison of symmetric and asymmetric algorithms including AES internals, RSA operations, ECC advantages, and hybrid encryption.
Foundational security design principles including economy of mechanism, least privilege, complete mediation, open design, and psychological acceptability.
How digital signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation using hash functions and asymmetric encryption.
Cryptographic hash functions, HMAC, message authentication codes, and their role in ensuring data integrity.
PKI components, certificate lifecycle, trust models, certificate types, and PKI vulnerabilities.
Security challenges and controls for virtualized environments including hypervisor security, VM isolation, container security, and virtual network security.
Securing SCADA, ICS, and OT environments including Purdue model, protocol security, and IT/OT convergence challenges.

topics.t: Physical Security Integration with Logical Controls
topics.d: How physical security controls complement logical/technical controls and the importance of converged security programs.
Security challenges and controls for embedded systems, IoT devices, and cyber-physical systems.
Security considerations for facility planning including site selection, building design, utility management, and environmental controls.
Methods of attacking cryptographic systems including brute force, mathematical attacks, implementation attacks, and social engineering.

topics.t: Zero Knowledge Proofs and Advanced Cryptographic Protocols
topics.d: Advanced cryptographic concepts including zero knowledge proofs, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and post-quantum cryptography.

topics.t: Secure Architecture Principles: Defense in Depth and Least Privilege
topics.d: Defense in depth layers multiple independent security controls so no single failure compromises the system. Least privilege restricts access to the minimum necessary. Together they form the foundation of secure architecture.

topics.t: Security Models: Brewer-Nash, Graham-Denning, and Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman
topics.d: Beyond Bell-LaPadula and Biba, additional security models address specific access control scenarios: Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) for conflicts of interest, Graham-Denning for access rights creation, and HRU for access control decidability.

Covert channels are unauthorized communication paths that violate the system security policy. Storage channels transmit data by modifying shared resources. Timing channels use variations in processing time to signal information.

topics.t: Cryptographic Algorithm Comparison: AES, RSA, ECC, SHA
topics.d: Understanding the strengths, key sizes, performance characteristics, and appropriate use cases for major cryptographic algorithms is essential for the CISSP exam.
X.509 digital certificates bind a public key to an identity. The certificate lifecycle includes request, issuance, use, renewal, suspension, and revocation. CRLs and OCSP check certificate validity.

Steganography hides the existence of a message within another medium (image, audio, video). Digital watermarking embeds identifying information for traceability. Both complement but differ from encryption.

topics.t: Fire Suppression Systems for Data Centers
topics.d: Fire suppression in data centers requires systems that extinguish fires without damaging electronic equipment or harming personnel. Clean agent systems (FM-200, Novec 1230) are preferred over water-based systems.

TEMPEST is a US government program addressing the security risk of electromagnetic emanations from electronic equipment. Countermeasures include shielding (Faraday cages), filtering, masking, and distance.

topics.t: Cloud Security Architecture and Deployment Models
topics.d: Cloud deployment models (public, private, hybrid, community) and service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) create different security responsibilities. Understanding multi-tenancy risks and cloud-specific threats is essential.

topics.t: Secure Boot and Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
topics.d: Secure boot ensures only authorized software loads during startup. TPM provides hardware-based security functions including key storage, attestation, and integrity measurement. Together they establish trust from hardware up.

topics.t: Industrial Control Systems and SCADA Security
topics.d: ICS/SCADA systems control critical infrastructure (power, water, manufacturing). They have unique security challenges including legacy protocols, long lifecycles, and safety-critical requirements that differ from IT security.

Memory protection prevents processes from accessing memory outside their allocated space. Key mechanisms include ASLR, DEP/NX, stack canaries, and bounds checking. These defenses mitigate buffer overflow attacks.

topics.t: Database Encryption: TDE, Column-Level, and Application-Level
topics.d: Databases can be encrypted at different granularities: Transparent Data Encryption (full database), column-level (specific sensitive fields), and application-level (encrypted before database storage). Each has different security and performance trade-offs.

topics.t: Lattice-Based Access Control and Mandatory Access Control
topics.d: Lattice models define mathematical upper and lower bounds for access control decisions. MAC enforces system-wide security policy based on classifications and clearances, not owner discretion.

Wireless networks require specific security architectures: 802.1X for enterprise authentication, EAP for flexible credential exchange, and proper encryption (WPA3) to protect data confidentiality over the air.

The Clark-Wilson model enforces integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties. It uses constrained data items (CDIs), transformation procedures (TPs), and integrity verification procedures (IVPs).

topics.t: Common Criteria and Evaluation Assurance Levels
topics.d: The Common Criteria (ISO 15408) provides an international framework for evaluating IT security products. Products are evaluated against Protection Profiles using Evaluation Assurance Levels (EAL1-7).

Key management is often the weakest link in cryptographic systems. The key lifecycle includes generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, archival, and destruction. HSMs provide hardware-protected key storage.

Physical security uses concentric layers of controls from perimeter to interior. Each layer provides deterrence, detection, delay, and response. Understanding control placement and integration with logical security is essential.

Blockchain provides an immutable, distributed ledger using cryptographic hashing and consensus mechanisms. Understanding security properties, vulnerabilities, and appropriate use cases is increasingly relevant.

EDR solutions monitor endpoint activity in real-time, detect suspicious behavior, and enable rapid response. Understanding EDR capabilities, deployment, and how it complements traditional antivirus is essential.

topics.t: Supply Chain Attacks and Third-Party Risk in Operations
topics.d: Supply chain attacks target the weakest link in the chain of vendors, suppliers, and service providers. Third-party risk management requires due diligence, contractual protections, and continuous monitoring.

Quantum computers threaten current cryptographic algorithms. RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman are vulnerable to quantum attacks using Shor's algorithm. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) develops quantum-resistant algorithms.
Zero Trust eliminates implicit trust based on network location. Every access request is verified regardless of where it originates. NIST SP 800-207 defines the Zero Trust Architecture framework.

Virtualization introduces unique security challenges including hypervisor attacks, VM escape, VM sprawl, and inter-VM communication risks. Proper security requires hardening the hypervisor and controlling the virtual environment.
Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) provides equivalent security to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes, making it ideal for mobile and IoT devices with limited resources.
Side-channel attacks extract secret information by analyzing physical characteristics of cryptographic implementations: timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, and acoustic signals.

topics.t: PKI Trust Models and Certificate Path Validation
topics.d: PKI trust models define how entities establish trust in digital certificates. Models include hierarchical, mesh, bridge, and web of trust. Certificate path validation ensures the chain from entity to trust anchor is valid.

Ransomware defense requires a multi-layered strategy: prevention (patch, segment, train), detection (EDR, behavioral monitoring), and recovery (offline backups, tested restoration procedures). Paying ransom is discouraged.

topics.t: OSI and TCP/IP Models in Depth
topics.d: OSI has 7 layers; TCP/IP has 4 layers. Each layer has specific protocols, data units, and devices. Encapsulation adds headers going down; decapsulation removes them going up. Understanding layer mapping is essential for attack identification and device placement.

topics.t: Network Attacks: DDoS, MITM, DNS Poisoning
topics.d: DDoS floods targets with traffic from botnets. MITM intercepts communications between two parties. DNS poisoning corrupts name resolution to redirect traffic. ARP spoofing redirects local traffic. Each attack targets specific layers and has specific countermeasures.

1st gen: Packet filter (stateless, L3). 2nd gen: Application proxy (L7, most secure, slowest) and Circuit-level (L5, SOCKS). 3rd gen: Stateful (L3-4, tracks connections). NGFW: multi-function (IDS/IPS, TLS inspection, application awareness).

topics.t: Wireless Security: WPA3, EAP, and Enterprise Authentication
topics.d: WEP is broken (24-bit IV, RC4). WPA2 uses AES-CCMP. WPA3 adds SAE (Dragonfly) for forward secrecy and offline attack resistance. Enterprise wireless uses 802.1X with EAP variants (PEAP, EAP-TLS). Rogue APs and evil twins are primary wireless threats.

Network segmentation divides networks into zones to limit lateral movement. VLANs provide logical separation at Layer 2. DMZ isolates public-facing services. Micro-segmentation applies granular policies to individual workloads. SDN separates control and data planes for programmable security.

topics.t: VPN Technologies: IPsec, SSL/TLS, and Tunneling Protocols
topics.d: VPNs create encrypted tunnels over untrusted networks. IPsec operates at Layer 3 (AH for integrity, ESP for encryption), SSL/TLS VPNs operate at Layer 4-7. Key protocols include IKE for key exchange, and tunneling modes (transport vs tunnel).

topics.t: Email Security Protocols: S/MIME, DKIM, SPF, DMARC
topics.d: Email security uses layered protocols: S/MIME and PGP for end-to-end message encryption and signing, SPF validates sender IP, DKIM adds cryptographic signatures to messages, and DMARC ties them together with policy enforcement.

topics.t: DNS Security: DNSSEC, DoH, DoT, and DNS Attacks
topics.d: DNS is critical infrastructure vulnerable to cache poisoning, DNS tunneling, and hijacking. DNSSEC adds digital signatures. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt DNS queries. DNS is the "phonebook of the internet."

topics.t: Content Delivery Networks (CDN) and Edge Security
topics.d: CDNs distribute content across global edge servers for performance and DDoS protection. They also provide WAF, bot management, and TLS termination. CDNs introduce security considerations around cache poisoning, origin protection, and SSL/TLS management.

NAC verifies device compliance before granting network access. 802.1X provides port-based authentication using EAP. NAC checks device health (patches, antivirus, encryption) and quarantines non-compliant devices.

topics.t: Network Device Security: Routers, Switches, and Load Balancers
topics.d: Network infrastructure devices must be hardened: disable unnecessary services, use encrypted management protocols, implement access control lists, and monitor for unauthorized changes. Each device type has specific security considerations.

Converged networks carry data, voice, and video on a single infrastructure. VoIP security concerns include eavesdropping, toll fraud, and DoS. Protocols include SIP, H.323, SRTP. Converged networks require QoS, VLAN separation, and encryption.

topics.t: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV)
topics.d: SDN separates the control plane from the data plane for programmable, centralized network management. NFV virtualizes network functions (firewalls, load balancers) as software. Both enable agile security but introduce new attack surfaces.

topics.t: Secure Communication Protocols: SSH, TLS 1.3, and IPsec
topics.d: SSH provides encrypted remote access (port 22). TLS 1.3 is the latest secure transport protocol. IPsec provides Layer 3 network encryption. Each has specific use cases, strengths, and configuration requirements.

topics.t: Network Monitoring: IDS, IPS, and SIEM Integration
topics.d: IDS detects intrusions (passive). IPS prevents intrusions (inline). Types: NIDS/NIPS (network) and HIDS/HIPS (host). Detection methods: signature-based (known threats), anomaly-based (deviations from baseline), and heuristic (behavioral patterns).

IPv6 expands the address space to 128 bits, includes built-in IPsec support, uses NDP instead of ARP, and introduces new security considerations including neighbor discovery attacks, tunneling risks, and dual-stack vulnerabilities.

Wireless attacks include rogue APs, evil twins, deauthentication attacks, WPS brute force, and Bluetooth attacks (Bluejacking, Bluesnarfing, Bluebugging). Countermeasures include WIPS, 802.1X, and wireless security policies.

topics.t: Network Architecture: DMZ, Bastion Hosts, and Screened Subnets
topics.d: Network architecture uses zones of trust: internal (trusted), DMZ (semi-trusted), external (untrusted). Bastion hosts are hardened systems exposed to untrusted networks. Screened subnet architecture uses routers and firewalls for layered protection.

topics.t: Secure Network Protocols and Port Numbers
topics.d: Critical port numbers and their security implications. Secure protocols replace insecure ones: SSH (22) replaces Telnet (23), SFTP/SCP replace FTP (21), HTTPS (443) replaces HTTP (80), LDAPS (636) replaces LDAP (389).
Understanding how protocols interact across OSI layers and the security implications of protocol encapsulation, tunneling, and covert channels.
Implementing granular network segmentation at the workload level to enforce least-privilege network access in modern data centers and cloud environments.
Securing email communication through authentication, encryption, and anti-spoofing protocols including SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and S/MIME.

topics.t: WAN Technologies and Circuit-Switched vs Packet-Switched Networks
topics.d: Understanding WAN connectivity options including dedicated circuits, packet-switched networks, MPLS, SD-WAN, and their security implications.
Security considerations for CDNs, web caches, proxy servers, and content delivery architectures including cache poisoning and edge security.

topics.t: Network Traffic Analysis and Flow Monitoring
topics.d: Techniques for monitoring and analyzing network traffic patterns including NetFlow, sFlow, packet capture, and traffic baseline analysis.
Implementing pre-admission and post-admission network access controls using 802.1X, NAC agents, health checks, and remediation networks.
Security architecture of cellular networks from 3G through 5G, including mobile communication protocols, IMSI catchers, and mobile device threats.

topics.t: Load Balancing and High Availability Networking
topics.d: Network-level high availability through load balancers, clustering, failover mechanisms, and redundant network architectures.

topics.t: Secure Remote Access and VPN Architectures
topics.d: VPN technologies, remote access architectures, and secure connectivity solutions including IPsec, SSL/TLS VPN, split tunneling, and always-on VPN.
Common network-level attacks including DDoS, ARP spoofing, VLAN hopping, man-in-the-middle, and BGP hijacking with their countermeasures.
Security considerations for satellite communications, Li-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, RFID, and other alternative communication technologies.
Evolution of firewall technologies from packet filters through next-generation firewalls, including deployment architectures and selection criteria.
Designing secure network architectures using VLANs, DMZs, screened subnets, bastion hosts, and network segmentation strategies.
Comprehensive review of wireless protocols from WEP through WPA3, wireless attacks, and enterprise wireless security deployment.
DNS infrastructure security including DNSSEC, DNS over HTTPS/TLS, DNS attacks, and protective DNS services.
Security implications of SDN including controller security, API protection, programmable security policies, and SDN-specific threats.
Securing voice, video, messaging, and collaboration platforms including VoIP, SIP, and conferencing security.
Network security in cloud environments including VPCs, security groups, transit gateways, and cloud-native network controls.
Security weaknesses in common network protocols including ARP, BGP, ICMP, and SNMP with attack vectors and mitigations.

TCP/IP protocols were designed for reliability, not security. Understanding TCP three-way handshake, SYN floods, session hijacking, IP spoofing, and protocol-level attacks is essential for the CISSP exam.

Network segmentation divides the network into zones with different security levels. Strategies include VLANs, subnets, DMZs, micro-segmentation, and zero trust network access. Segmentation limits lateral movement after a breach.

TLS 1.3 significantly improves upon previous versions with faster handshake, mandatory forward secrecy, and removal of weak algorithms. Understanding protocol evolution and configuration best practices is essential.

topics.t: Wireless Security: WPA3, EAP Methods, and Attack Vectors
topics.d: Wireless security has evolved from WEP (broken) through WPA/WPA2 to WPA3. Understanding authentication methods (EAP types), encryption protocols, and wireless-specific attacks is critical.

IPv6 introduces security changes: mandatory IPsec support (but not mandatory use), larger address space reducing scanning, but new attack surfaces including NDP attacks, extension header abuse, and dual-stack vulnerabilities.

NIDS/NIPS detect and prevent network attacks using signature-based, anomaly-based, and stateful protocol analysis methods. Understanding detection methods, deployment placement, and limitations is critical.

topics.t: VPN Technologies: IPsec, SSL/TLS, and WireGuard
topics.d: VPNs create encrypted tunnels over untrusted networks. IPsec operates at Layer 3 for site-to-site VPNs. SSL/TLS VPNs work at Layer 4-7 for remote access. WireGuard is a modern alternative with simpler design.

Distributed Denial of Service attacks overwhelm targets through volumetric (bandwidth), protocol (state table), or application-layer (resource) attacks. Defense requires multi-layered mitigation including ISP scrubbing, CDN, and WAF.

topics.t: Email Security: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and S/MIME
topics.d: Email authentication protocols (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) prevent spoofing and phishing. S/MIME provides end-to-end email encryption and signing. Together they address the major email security threats.

topics.t: SDN and Network Function Virtualization Security
topics.d: Software-Defined Networking separates the control plane from the data plane, centralizing network management. NFV virtualizes network functions (firewalls, load balancers). Both introduce new security considerations.

topics.t: Secure Network Architecture: Bastion Hosts, Screened Subnets, and Proxy Servers
topics.d: Secure network architectures use bastion hosts (hardened public-facing systems), screened subnets (DMZ with dual firewalls), and proxy servers (intermediaries hiding internal systems) to protect internal resources.

Understanding which security protocols and attacks operate at each OSI layer is fundamental. Each layer has specific vulnerabilities, protocols, and countermeasures that the CISSP exam tests extensively.

topics.t: Network Address Translation and Its Security Implications
topics.d: NAT translates private IP addresses to public addresses, providing a form of security by obscuring internal network topology. However, NAT is not a security control and has implications for IPsec, VoIP, and IPv6 transition.

DNS is critical infrastructure vulnerable to spoofing, cache poisoning, and amplification attacks. DNSSEC provides authentication and integrity. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) provide confidentiality.

topics.t: Network Monitoring: NetFlow, sFlow, and Packet Capture
topics.d: Network monitoring tools provide different levels of visibility. NetFlow/sFlow provide metadata about traffic flows. Full packet capture provides complete content. Each serves different security monitoring needs.

topics.t: Cloud Networking and Virtual Network Security
topics.d: Cloud networking uses virtual constructs (VPCs, subnets, security groups, NACLs) that require different security approaches than physical networks. Understanding these constructs is essential for cloud security.

Internet of Things (IoT) devices expand the attack surface with constrained resources, infrequent patching, default credentials, and long deployment lifetimes. Securing IoT requires lightweight cryptography, network segmentation, and lifecycle management.

Bluetooth, NFC, and other short-range wireless protocols have unique security vulnerabilities including eavesdropping, MITM attacks, and device tracking. Understanding attack vectors and mitigations is essential.

topics.t: Content Distribution Networks and Edge Security
topics.d: CDNs distribute content across geographically dispersed edge servers, improving performance and resilience. CDN security includes DDoS mitigation, WAF integration, TLS termination, and origin protection.

WAN technologies connect geographically distributed sites. Understanding MPLS, SD-WAN, leased lines, and their security properties helps architects choose appropriate connectivity for different security requirements.

topics.d: IAAA establishes accountability. Four factor types: Type 1 (know — password), Type 2 (have — token), Type 3 (are — biometric), Type 4 (where — location). MFA requires 2+ different types.

topics.t: Biometric Authentication: FRR, FAR, and CER
topics.d: Biometrics authenticate based on physical or behavioral characteristics. FRR (Type 1 Error) rejects legitimate users. FAR (Type 2 Error) accepts imposters. CER (Crossover Error Rate) where FAR equals FRR is the primary accuracy metric — lower CER means more accurate.

topics.t: Identity Lifecycle and Privileged Access Management
topics.d: Identity lifecycle: Provisioning → Management → Deprovisioning. Provisioning must follow least privilege. Deprovisioning must be immediate upon termination. Privileged Access Management (PAM) controls admin accounts through vaulting, session recording, JIT elevation, and zero standing privileges.

topics.t: SSO and Federation: SAML, OAuth, OpenID Connect
topics.d: SAML provides enterprise SSO using XML assertions between IdP and SP. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework using access tokens. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of OAuth. XACML defines access control policies. Federation enables cross-organization trust.

Kerberos v5 uses KDC (AS+TGS) for ticket-based authentication with symmetric encryption (AES). KDC is single point of failure. RADIUS: UDP, encrypts password only, combines AAA. TACACS+: TCP, encrypts everything, separates AAA. Diameter: not backward-compatible with RADIUS.

topics.t: Access Control Models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC
topics.d: DAC: owner decides (flexible, least secure). MAC: system-enforced labels (rigid, most secure). RBAC: role-based (most common in enterprise). ABAC: attribute-based (most flexible, supports complex policies). Rule-based uses if/then rules (firewalls). Implicit deny is the most secure default.

topics.t: Identity Provisioning, Deprovisioning, and Access Reviews
topics.d: Identity provisioning creates and manages user accounts throughout the identity lifecycle. Deprovisioning removes access when no longer needed. Regular access reviews (recertification) ensure least privilege is maintained over time.

MFA requires two or more different factor types: something you know (Type 1), something you have (Type 2), something you are (Type 3). Two factors of the same type is NOT MFA. MFA dramatically reduces credential compromise attacks.

Common attacks against access controls include password attacks (brute force, dictionary, rainbow tables), privilege escalation, session hijacking, and credential stuffing. Each has specific countermeasures.

Directory services (Active Directory, LDAP) provide centralized identity management. LDAP (port 389, LDAPS port 636) queries directory data using a hierarchical structure (DN, OU, CN). Active Directory integrates Kerberos, LDAP, DNS, and Group Policy.

Effective credential management includes strong password policies, password managers, credential vaulting, and modern passwordless alternatives. NIST SP 800-63B updated password guidance significantly — no forced rotation, no composition rules.

Zero Trust applies identity-centric security: every access request is verified regardless of network location. Core components include continuous authentication, device trust evaluation, micro-segmentation, and least privilege access with JIT/JEA.

Session management controls how authenticated sessions are created, maintained, and terminated. Secure session tokens must be random, unpredictable, and protected. JWT, SAML tokens, and cookies each have specific security requirements.

Federation enables authentication across organizational boundaries. Trust relationships allow users from one domain to access resources in another. Standards include SAML, OAuth, OIDC, and WS-Federation. Cross-certification and trusted third-party models.

Accountability links actions to identities through logging, auditing, and monitoring. Audit trails must be protected, comprehensive, and regularly reviewed. Non-repudiation ensures actions cannot be denied.
Controls and tools for managing, monitoring, and securing privileged accounts including password vaulting, session recording, just-in-time access, and privilege elevation.
Detailed analysis of access control models including DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC, Rule-Based, and Risk-Based access control with implementation considerations.
Deep dive into biometric authentication including physiological and behavioral biometrics, error rates, anti-spoofing, and emerging authentication technologies.
Managing identity from creation through modification to decommissioning, including provisioning, access reviews, role transitions, and deprovisioning.

topics.t: Service Accounts and Non-Human Identity Management
topics.d: Managing machine identities including service accounts, API keys, certificates, managed identities, and workload identity in cloud-native environments.
Physical access control technologies including smart cards, proximity cards, mantrap/airlock, turnstiles, bollards, and convergence of physical and logical access.
Technical implementation of authorization including ACLs, capability tables, security labels, content-dependent and context-dependent controls, and policy decision/enforcement points.
SSO implementation approaches including Kerberos-based, SAML-based, OIDC-based, and agent-based SSO with security considerations.
Processes for ensuring access remains appropriate over time including user access reviews, role mining, segregation of duties enforcement, and identity governance.
Securing directory services including LDAP, Active Directory, schema security, replication security, and directory-based attacks.
Emerging authentication technologies including FIDO2/WebAuthn, passkeys, behavioral biometrics, and risk-adaptive authentication.
Managing identities in cloud environments including IAM roles, temporary credentials, cross-account access, and cloud-native identity controls.
Secure storage, rotation, and lifecycle management of credentials including passwords, API keys, certificates, and secrets vaults.
Cross-organizational identity sharing using SAML, OAuth, OIDC, and trust frameworks enabling SSO across domains.
Secure creation, maintenance, and termination of user sessions including token management, timeout policies, and session hijacking prevention.
Verifying the identity of individuals before issuing credentials, including NIST SP 800-63A identity assurance levels and enrollment processes.
Logging, monitoring, and auditing identity and access activities to ensure accountability, detect anomalies, and support compliance.
Centralized vs decentralized administration, provisioning workflows, access request processes, and delegated administration models.

topics.t: Identity as a Service and Cloud Identity
topics.d: Cloud-based identity services including IDaaS, SCIM provisioning, directory synchronization, and multi-cloud identity strategies.
Architecture and implementation of MFA including factor selection, risk-based authentication, step-up authentication, and MFA bypass prevention.
Preventing unauthorized elevation of access rights through technical controls, monitoring, and least privilege enforcement.
Common attacks against access control systems including pass-the-hash, Kerberoasting, token manipulation, and relay attacks with defenses.
Zero trust identity principles including continuous verification, microsegmentation, policy enforcement points, and identity-centric security.

Kerberos is a symmetric-key authentication protocol using a trusted third party (KDC). It provides SSO through ticket-based authentication. Understanding the authentication flow, components, and limitations is heavily tested.

AAA protocols authenticate, authorize, and account for network access. RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only passwords. TACACS+ uses TCP and encrypts the entire payload. Diameter is the successor to RADIUS.

OAuth 2.0 provides delegated authorization (not authentication). OpenID Connect adds authentication on top of OAuth. SAML is an XML-based SSO protocol for enterprise federation. Understanding when to use each is critical.

topics.t: Access Control Models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, and ABAC
topics.d: Four primary access control models determine how access decisions are made. DAC uses owner discretion, MAC uses system-enforced labels, RBAC uses job roles, and ABAC uses attributes for fine-grained control.
Biometric authentication uses physiological or behavioral characteristics. Key metrics are FRR, FAR, and CER. Understanding biometric types, accuracy trade-offs, and attack vectors is essential.

topics.t: Privilege Escalation and Privileged Access Management
topics.d: Privilege escalation attacks gain elevated access (vertical = admin, horizontal = another user). PAM solutions control, monitor, and audit privileged access through vaulting, session recording, and just-in-time access.

Identity federation enables users from one organization to access resources in another without separate credentials. Trust relationships, assertion protocols, and cross-domain identity management require careful security consideration.

Access control administration includes provisioning, review, and deprovisioning. Regular access reviews (recertification) detect privilege creep. Automated tools enforce timely deprovisioning upon role changes or termination.

FIDO2 (WebAuthn + CTAP) enables passwordless authentication using public key cryptography and hardware authenticators. It eliminates password-related attacks including phishing, credential stuffing, and password reuse.
ABAC evaluates access requests based on attributes of the subject, object, action, and environment. Policies combine multiple attributes for fine-grained, context-aware access decisions.

IGA platforms manage the full identity lifecycle: provisioning, access requests, access certification, separation of duties enforcement, and analytics. IGA ensures the right people have the right access at the right time.

MFA combines two or more authentication factors from different categories. Understanding factor types, MFA bypass attacks, and adaptive/risk-based authentication helps select appropriate MFA strategies.

Accountability ensures actions can be traced to responsible individuals through audit trails, logging, and monitoring. Non-repudiation prevents denial of actions. Understanding what to log and how to protect logs is critical.

Modern password policies focus on length over complexity. Credential storage must use adaptive hashing algorithms (bcrypt, Argon2) with unique salts. Understanding password attacks and defenses is essential.
LDAP directories provide centralized identity storage for authentication and authorization. Understanding LDAP structure, LDAP injection attacks, and secure LDAP configuration is important for IAM.

Service accounts, API keys, certificates, and machine identities are non-human credentials that require special management. They often have elevated privileges and are frequently overlooked in security programs.
Session management controls the lifecycle of user sessions from creation to termination. Secure session handling prevents hijacking, fixation, and replay attacks.
Directory services (Active Directory, LDAP) are central authentication and authorization infrastructure. Compromising the directory service compromises the entire organization.

Decentralized identity gives individuals control over their digital identities without relying on centralized identity providers. Verifiable credentials and blockchain-based identifiers enable self-sovereign identity.
Conditional access policies evaluate risk signals at authentication time to make dynamic access decisions. Factors include device compliance, location, risk score, and behavior patterns.
