name: Security Assessment and Testing

topics.d: Test = verify one control. Assessment = comprehensive review + recommendations. Audit = formal review by auditors. Internal audits serve stakeholders; external audits by Big 4 serve regulators. SOC 1 = financial controls, SOC 2 = security/trust, SOC 3 = public summary.

Vulnerability assessment identifies weaknesses without exploiting them. Penetration testing actively exploits vulnerabilities to prove impact. VA is broader coverage; pen testing is deeper analysis. Both require written authorization. VA runs regularly; pen tests are periodic.

topics.t: Code Review Methods: SAST, DAST, and Fagan Inspection
topics.d: SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes source code without execution — finds buffer overflows, injection flaws. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests running applications — finds XSS, SQLi, authentication flaws. Fagan Inspection (POPIR-F) is the most formal manual code review. IAST combines both approaches.

topics.t: SCAP, Log Reviews, and Continuous Monitoring
topics.d: SCAP (NIST) standardizes vulnerability management: CVE (names), CVSS (scores 0-10), CCE (configs), CPE (platforms), XCCDF (checklists), OVAL (testing). Log reviews detect anomalies and policy violations. SIEM aggregates and correlates logs. Continuous monitoring provides ongoing security posture awareness.

Fuzz testing sends random or semi-random input to find crashes and vulnerabilities. Mutation fuzzing (dumb) modifies existing inputs randomly. Generational fuzzing (intelligent) creates inputs from a data model — finds more subtle bugs. Synthetic transactions test systems with scripted scenarios to verify expected behavior.

topics.t: SOC Reports, Third-Party Audits, and Compliance Validation
topics.d: SOC (System and Organization Controls) reports provide independent assurance of a service organization's controls. SOC 1 covers financial reporting, SOC 2 covers security/availability/processing integrity/confidentiality/privacy (Trust Services Criteria). Type I = design only, Type II = design + operational effectiveness over time.

topics.t: Penetration Testing Methodologies and Rules of Engagement
topics.d: Penetration testing simulates real attacks to identify exploitable vulnerabilities. Methodologies include OWASP, PTES, OSSTMM. Rules of engagement define scope, timing, and boundaries. Types: white box (full knowledge), gray box (partial), black box (no knowledge).

Vulnerability management is a continuous lifecycle: discover assets, scan for vulnerabilities, prioritize by risk, remediate or accept, verify fixes, and report. It is not a one-time scan but an ongoing program with metrics and governance.

Security audits independently verify control effectiveness. Types: internal (organization's own team), external (independent third party), regulatory (government agency). Standards include ISO 19011, ISACA audit standards, and AICPA standards.

SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) standardizes automated security assessment. Components: CVE (vulnerability naming), CVSS (scoring), CCE (configuration), CPE (platform naming), XCCDF (checklist format), OVAL (test language).

Software testing encompasses unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and acceptance testing. Security-specific methods include fuzzing, static analysis (SAST), dynamic analysis (DAST), interactive testing (IAST), and regression testing.

topics.t: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and Security Metrics
topics.d: Meaningful security metrics drive improvement and demonstrate program effectiveness. Key metrics include MTTD, MTTR, patch compliance, vulnerability aging, phishing click rate, and cost per incident. Metrics must be actionable, not just collected.

Continuous monitoring provides real-time visibility into security posture through automated scanning, log analysis, configuration monitoring, and threat detection. NIST SP 800-137 defines the continuous monitoring program.

topics.t: Code Review and Software Testing Techniques
topics.d: Comprehensive review of code analysis methods including static analysis, dynamic analysis, code reviews, walkthroughs, and formal inspection processes.
Structured approach to penetration testing including planning, reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation, and reporting with rules of engagement.
Measuring security program effectiveness through Key Performance Indicators, Key Risk Indicators, metrics frameworks, and security dashboards.
Centralized log collection, aggregation, correlation, and analysis using SIEM platforms for security monitoring, alerting, and compliance.
Automated vulnerability scanning tools, techniques, scan types, and vulnerability management lifecycle from discovery through remediation.
Testing security controls against regulatory requirements including PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOX, GDPR compliance assessment, and audit preparation.

topics.t: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Testing
topics.d: Testing BCP/DRP through tabletop exercises, walkthroughs, simulations, parallel tests, and full-interruption tests with lessons learned integration.
Evaluating security architectures through threat modeling, design reviews, attack surface analysis, and architecture risk assessment.

topics.t: Security Control Validation and Effectiveness Testing
topics.d: Methods for validating that security controls are operating as intended including control testing, red team assessments, and tabletop exercises.

topics.t: Data Collection and Analysis for Security Testing
topics.d: Collecting and analyzing security data from multiple sources including vulnerability databases, threat feeds, log analysis, and security information sharing.

topics.t: Interface Testing and Misuse Case Analysis
topics.d: Testing system interfaces, APIs, and user interactions for security vulnerabilities including negative testing, boundary testing, and abuse case development.

topics.t: Security Assessment Reporting and Risk Communication
topics.d: Effectively communicating security assessment findings to technical and business audiences through structured reports, risk ratings, and remediation recommendations.
Evaluating the security posture of third-party service providers through questionnaires, audits, certifications, and continuous monitoring.
Planning, conducting, and reporting security audits including internal audits, external audits, regulatory audits, and audit evidence collection.
Real-time and ongoing monitoring of security controls using automated tools, dashboards, and risk-based alerting.
Testing software for security vulnerabilities including unit testing, integration testing, regression testing, and acceptance testing with security focus.
Frameworks for selecting, implementing, and measuring security controls including NIST 800-53, ISO 27002, CIS Controls, and COBIT.
Identifying, measuring, and reducing the attack surface through systematic enumeration of entry points, trust boundaries, and exposure.
Managing vulnerability disclosure programs including bug bounty platforms, responsible disclosure policies, and coordinated vulnerability disclosure.
Structured approaches to security assessment including OWASP Testing Guide, NIST SP 800-115, PTES, and OSSTMM.
Tracking organizational compliance with regulatory requirements, industry standards, and internal policies through monitoring and reporting.
Quantifying how well security controls achieve their objectives through testing, metrics, and maturity assessment.
Using forensic techniques for security assessments including evidence collection, analysis tools, and forensic readiness.

Vulnerability assessments systematically identify weaknesses in systems, networks, and applications. Understanding scanner types, CVSS scoring, false positives/negatives, and assessment frequency is essential.

topics.t: Penetration Testing: Types, Phases, and Rules of Engagement
topics.d: Penetration testing simulates real attacks to test security controls. Types include black box, white box, and grey box. The ROE document defines scope, authorization, and constraints. Understanding the testing lifecycle is critical.
Security audits verify compliance and control effectiveness. Types include internal, external, and third-party audits. Key standards include SOC 1/2/3, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS QSA assessments.

topics.t: Software Testing Methods: SAST, DAST, IAST, and SCA
topics.d: Application security testing uses complementary methods: SAST (static — source code), DAST (dynamic — running application), IAST (interactive — instrumented runtime), and SCA (software composition analysis — third-party components).

Log management collects, stores, and analyzes log data from across the enterprise. SIEM correlates events from multiple sources to detect threats. Understanding log types, retention, and correlation rules is essential.

topics.t: Code Review Techniques: Fagan Inspection and Peer Review
topics.d: Formal code review (Fagan inspection) is the most effective method for finding defects. Peer reviews, walkthroughs, and automated reviews complement formal inspections at different cost and thoroughness levels.
Security metrics quantify security posture and program effectiveness. KPIs measure performance against objectives. KRIs provide early warning of increasing risk. Metrics must be SMART and actionable.

Compliance testing verifies that security controls satisfy regulatory, contractual, and policy requirements. Methods include control testing, substantive testing, gap analysis, and evidence collection for auditors.
A vulnerability management program continuously identifies, classifies, prioritizes, remediates, and verifies vulnerabilities across the organization. It is a cyclical process, not a one-time scan.

Security control validation verifies that implemented controls actually work as intended. Methods include testing, red team exercises, purple team collaboration, and breach and attack simulation (BAS).

Effective security assessment reports communicate findings, risk, and recommendations to different audiences. Executive summaries address leadership, technical details address remediation teams, and risk ratings prioritize action.

Bug bounty programs invite external security researchers to find and responsibly disclose vulnerabilities in exchange for rewards. They complement internal security testing by leveraging diverse attacker perspectives.

topics.t: Red Team and Purple Team Operations
topics.d: Red teams simulate real-world adversaries to test organizational defenses end-to-end. Purple teams combine red team offense with blue team defense for collaborative security improvement.

Security control assessments verify that controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome. NIST SP 800-53A defines assessment methods: examine, interview, and test.

Continuous monitoring provides ongoing awareness of security posture through automated data collection, analysis, and reporting. NIST SP 800-137 defines the ISCM (Information Security Continuous Monitoring) strategy.
Third-party risk assessment evaluates the security posture of vendors, suppliers, and partners who have access to organizational data or systems. It is a critical component of supply chain security.
SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) provides standardized specifications for automated security assessment, including vulnerability checking, configuration compliance, and patch verification.

name: Security Operations

topics.d: Permission (access object) + Rights (take action) = Privilege. Need to Know = data access. Least Privilege = system privileges. SoD = preventive (prevents fraud). Job Rotation = detective (detects fraud). Mandatory Vacation = detective.

NIST 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity. The organization's 7-step model: Detect → Respond → Mitigate → Report → Recover → Remediate → Lessons Learned. Only designated spokesperson communicates with media.

Digital forensics follows: Identify → Preserve → Collect → Examine → Analyze → Report. Chain of custody documents who handled evidence and when. Volatile evidence (RAM, cache) must be collected first. Legal hold preserves ESI. Four evidence types: real, documentary, testimonial, demonstrative.

topics.t: Disaster Recovery: RPO, RTO, MTBF, MTTR
topics.d: RPO = maximum acceptable data loss (how far back). RTO = maximum acceptable downtime (how fast to recover). MTBF = average time between failures. MTTR = average time to repair. MTBF = MTTF + MTTR. Hot site = fastest recovery. Cold site = cheapest.

Change management: Request → Review → Approve → Test → Schedule → Document. Unauthorized changes impact AVAILABILITY. Configuration management maintains baselines. Patch management: Evaluate → Test → Approve → Deploy → Verify. Configuration baselines enable drift detection.

Cloud shared responsibility: SaaS = CSP maximum, IaaS = consumer maximum. SDN separates control from data plane. Information lifecycle: Create → Classify → Store → Use → Archive → Destroy. Media sanitization: Clear < Purge < Destroy (NIST 800-88).

Security logging captures events from systems, applications, and network devices. SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) aggregates, correlates, and analyzes logs in real-time. Key concepts include log integrity, retention, correlation rules, and SOAR for automated response.

topics.t: Investigations, Evidence Types, and Legal Requirements
topics.d: Security investigations follow specific procedures depending on type (criminal, civil, regulatory, administrative). Evidence must meet legal standards: relevant, reliable, sufficient, and permissible. The exclusionary rule, search warrants, and legal holds are key concepts.

Threat intelligence informs security operations through IOCs, TTPs, and threat actor profiling. Sources include OSINT, ISACs, commercial feeds, and government agencies. Intelligence must be operationalized through SIEM integration and automated response.

topics.t: Incident Response Team Roles and Communication
topics.d: IR teams require defined roles: incident commander, technical lead, communications officer, legal counsel, and HR. Communication plans must address internal stakeholders, external parties, media, regulators, and law enforcement.

Patch management is a structured process: identify applicable patches, test in non-production, deploy per priority, verify effectiveness, and document. Emergency patches may bypass normal change management but must be documented after the fact.

topics.t: Backup Strategies: Full, Incremental, Differential, and Cloud
topics.d: Backup strategies balance recovery speed, storage requirements, and RPO compliance. Full (complete copy), Incremental (changes since last backup), Differential (changes since last full). Cloud backup adds geographic diversity but introduces bandwidth and security considerations.

The SOC provides centralized security monitoring, detection, and response. SOC models include dedicated (internal), managed (outsourced MSSP), and hybrid. SOC operates 24/7 with tiered analysts and uses SIEM, SOAR, EDR, and threat intelligence.

DR planning ensures IT systems recover after disruptions. Key elements: DR plan documentation, testing schedules, recovery procedures, alternate processing sites, and data restoration. DR is a subset of BCP focused on IT recovery.

Malware categories include viruses (require host), worms (self-propagate), trojans (disguised), ransomware (encrypt for payment), rootkits (hide presence), spyware, adware, and fileless malware. Defense requires layered controls: prevention, detection, and response.

Physical security operations include access control (badges, guards, mantraps), surveillance (CCTV, motion sensors), visitor management, equipment security, and media handling. Physical controls support and complement technical controls.

Business resilience goes beyond DR to ensure the organization can adapt and operate through disruptions. Key concepts: high availability (eliminate single points of failure), fault tolerance (continue despite component failure), and organizational resilience.

topics.t: Digital Forensics Procedures and Evidence Handling
topics.d: Forensic investigation methodology including evidence collection, chain of custody, forensic imaging, analysis techniques, and legal admissibility requirements.
Processes for managing system configurations and changes including configuration baselines, change advisory boards, and rollback procedures.
Building and operating incident response teams, defining roles, establishing communication plans, and managing stakeholder coordination during incidents.
Operational processes for identifying, testing, deploying, and verifying patches across enterprise systems with rollback capabilities.

topics.t: Physical Security Controls and Environmental Protection
topics.d: Environmental controls including HVAC, fire suppression, power protection, and physical security measures for data centers and facilities.
Types of investigations, evidence standards, legal holds, eDiscovery, and coordination with law enforcement.
Designing and operating a SOC including tiered analyst model, runbooks, playbooks, threat hunting, and SOC metrics.
Secure handling, storage, transport, and destruction of media including NIST SP 800-88 guidelines for data sanitization at end of lifecycle.

topics.t: Disaster Recovery Strategy and Site Selection
topics.d: DR site types, selection criteria, recovery strategies, and the relationship between MTD/RTO/RPO and recovery capabilities.
Endpoint protection including EDR, application whitelisting, host-based firewalls, full disk encryption, and endpoint hardening.
Collection, analysis, and operationalization of threat intelligence including STIX/TAXII, threat feeds, and intelligence-driven defense.
Operational aspects of business continuity including plan activation, crisis management, emergency communications, and continuity exercises.
SOC design including staffing models, tool integration, alert triage, playbooks, and SOC maturity progression.
Comprehensive logging architecture including log sources, centralization, retention, correlation, and compliance requirements.
Techniques for analyzing malicious software including static analysis, dynamic analysis, sandboxing, and malware classification.
Implementing DR strategies including backup methods, replication technologies, cloud DR, and recovery testing procedures.
Securing system resources through hardening, configuration baselines, secure provisioning, and infrastructure as code.
Security practices for managing personnel including background checks, onboarding, termination procedures, and insider threat programs.
Defining, monitoring, and enforcing SLAs for security services including uptime guarantees, response times, and vendor management.
Managing physical infrastructure security including data center operations, environmental controls, fire suppression, and facility access.

NIST SP 800-61 defines four IR phases: Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, and Post-Incident Activity. Understanding each phase, team roles, and communication procedures is heavily tested.

Backup strategies (full, incremental, differential) provide data recovery capabilities. Understanding backup types, rotation schemes, storage requirements, and recovery testing is essential for BCP/DR.
Understanding malware categories (virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, rootkit, fileless), propagation methods, and analysis techniques (static, dynamic, sandbox) is essential for security operations.

Change management ensures that modifications to systems and configurations are authorized, tested, documented, and reversible. The Change Advisory Board (CAB) reviews changes to prevent unauthorized or disruptive modifications.

DR implementation includes selecting site types, establishing recovery procedures, conducting testing, and maintaining plans. Understanding site types, recovery sequence, and testing methods is critical for the exam.

topics.t: Security Operations Center (SOC) Design and Operations
topics.d: The SOC is the centralized function for monitoring, detecting, and responding to security events. Understanding SOC tiers, staffing models, tools, and operational workflows is essential.

topics.t: Investigations: Criminal, Civil, Administrative, and Regulatory
topics.d: Different investigation types have different standards of evidence, procedures, and outcomes. Understanding when to involve law enforcement, preserve evidence, and maintain chain of custody is critical.

Threat intelligence transforms raw data into actionable information about threats. Understanding intelligence types (strategic, tactical, operational), sources (OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT), and sharing frameworks (STIX/TAXII) is essential.
Patch management is the systematic process of identifying, testing, deploying, and verifying software patches. Timely patching reduces the attack surface, but uncontrolled patching can cause outages.

Configuration management maintains systems in a known-good state through baselines, change control, and drift detection. System hardening reduces the attack surface by removing unnecessary services, applying secure settings, and enforcing least functionality.

Containment stops the spread of an incident while preserving evidence. Strategies include network isolation, account disabling, and system quarantine. The choice of containment strategy depends on incident type and business impact.

DR testing validates that recovery procedures actually work. Five testing types range from least disruptive (checklist review) to most disruptive (full interruption). Regular testing is essential — untested plans will fail.

Digital forensics follows strict procedures to ensure evidence integrity and admissibility. Key principles: work on copies (never originals), maintain chain of custody, hash everything, and follow the volatility order.

topics.t: Disaster Recovery Site Types and Selection
topics.d: Disaster recovery sites provide alternate processing capability when the primary site is unavailable. Site types (hot, warm, cold, mobile, cloud) differ in cost, readiness time, and capabilities.
Operational security controls ensure day-to-day security through defined procedures for system operations, media handling, monitoring, and personnel management.

Vulnerability management is the continuous process of identifying, evaluating, remediating, and reporting on security vulnerabilities. Patch management ensures timely application of vendor-supplied fixes.
Business Continuity Planning (BCP) ensures critical business functions continue during and after a disaster. BCP encompasses BIA, strategy development, plan development, and regular testing.

topics.t: Security Information and Event Management Architecture
topics.d: SIEM systems collect, correlate, and analyze security events from across the enterprise to detect threats, support investigations, and meet compliance requirements.

SLAs define the expected level of service between parties. For security operations, SLAs cover uptime, response times, patch timelines, and incident handling. Monitoring and enforcing SLAs ensures accountability.

name: Software Development Security

topics.t: SDLC Security Integration and Development Models
topics.d: Security must be integrated into EVERY SDLC phase, not bolted on at the end. Requirements phase: security requirements + risk assessment. Design: threat modeling. Develop: secure coding + peer review. Test: SAST/DAST. Operate: monitoring + patch management. DevSecOps automates security in CI/CD.

OWASP Top 10 is the standard awareness document for web application security. Key vulnerabilities: Injection (SQLi, XSS), Broken Authentication, Sensitive Data Exposure, Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, SSRF. Each has specific countermeasures that are exam-testable.

topics.t: Database Security: SQL Injection, Polyinstantiation, and ACID
topics.d: RDBMS: Row=Tuple (Cardinality), Column=Attribute (Degree). ACID ensures transaction reliability. Normalization reduces redundancy (1NF→2NF→3NF cumulative). Polyinstantiation prevents inference attacks. SQL injection exploits dynamic queries. Views restrict database access.

topics.t: SW-CMM, OOP Concepts, and Software Assurance
topics.d: SW-CMM: Initial → Repeatable → Defined → Managed → Optimized (IRDMO). OOP: High cohesion GOOD, Low coupling GOOD. Change management applies to software configuration. Assurance = confidence that controls work correctly throughout the system lifecycle.

topics.t: Software Testing Types and Acquired Software Security
topics.d: Software testing spans unit through acceptance testing. Acquired software (COTS/open-source) requires supply chain security evaluation. Code signing verifies software integrity. API security requires authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and input validation.

DevSecOps integrates security into every phase of the DevOps lifecycle. CI/CD pipelines automate build, test, and deployment with security gates: SAST in code commit, SCA for dependencies, DAST in staging, container scanning, and infrastructure-as-code (IaC) security validation.

APIs are primary attack surfaces in modern applications. Security requires authentication (OAuth 2.0, API keys), authorization (scopes, RBAC), input validation, rate limiting, and API gateways. Microservices introduce service mesh security, mutual TLS, and east-west traffic concerns.

topics.t: Secure Coding Practices and Input Validation
topics.d: Secure coding prevents vulnerabilities at the source. Key practices: input validation (whitelist), output encoding, parameterized queries, error handling, least privilege, and defense in depth. Never trust user input.

OOP principles affect security: Encapsulation (hiding internal state), Inheritance (extending classes — can inherit vulnerabilities), Polymorphism (methods behave differently by context), and Abstraction (hiding complexity). Understanding these enables secure design.

topics.t: Database Security: Views, Stored Procedures, and Aggregation
topics.d: Database security beyond SQL injection includes: views (restrict data visibility), stored procedures (controlled operations), aggregation attacks (combining low-level data reveals high-level secrets), inference attacks (deducing classified info from unclassified data).

topics.t: Software Acquisition and Third-Party Code Security
topics.d: Most software includes third-party components (open source, commercial libraries). Security requires: evaluating vendor security practices, maintaining SBOM, monitoring for vulnerabilities, and managing end-of-life software risks.

topics.t: Secure Development Environments and Change Control
topics.d: Separate development, testing, and production environments. Developers should NOT have production access. Code promotion follows formal processes. Version control, code review, and separation of duties protect code integrity.

HTTP security headers protect against common web attacks. Key headers: Content-Security-Policy (CSP), X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy.

topics.t: SDLC Models: Waterfall, Agile, Spiral, and DevOps
topics.d: Different SDLC models integrate security differently. Waterfall (sequential, requirements upfront), Agile (iterative, security in each sprint), Spiral (risk-driven, risk analysis each cycle), DevOps/DevSecOps (continuous, automated security).

Mobile app security concerns include insecure data storage, weak server-side controls, insufficient transport security, and reverse engineering. OWASP Mobile Top 10 guides mobile security. Controls include code obfuscation, certificate pinning, and secure data storage.
Securing APIs through authentication, authorization, rate limiting, input validation, and securing microservice-to-microservice communication.
Integrating security into DevOps practices through automated security testing, infrastructure as code scanning, container security, and secure deployment pipelines.
Securing the software supply chain including third-party libraries, open-source components, SBOM, dependency management, and supply chain attack prevention.
Design patterns that enhance security including defense in depth, fail-secure defaults, separation of privilege, and secure error handling.
The most critical web application security risks including injection, broken authentication, XSS, insecure deserialization, and server-side request forgery.
Coding standards including CERT Secure Coding, OWASP guidelines, defensive programming, memory safety, and error handling best practices.

topics.t: Data Warehousing and Big Data Security
topics.d: Security considerations for data warehouses, data lakes, big data platforms, and analytics environments including access control and privacy.

topics.t: Database Security and SQL Injection Prevention
topics.d: Securing database systems including access controls, encryption, SQL injection prevention, and database activity monitoring.
Security considerations for mobile application development including platform-specific controls, data storage, and communication security.
Security considerations when acquiring software including COTS evaluation, open-source risk, licensing, and vendor security assessment.
Security integration across development models including Waterfall, Agile, DevOps, and Spiral with security activities for each phase.

topics.t: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Security
topics.d: Security implications of AI/ML systems including adversarial attacks, model security, data poisoning, and responsible AI.

topics.t: Code Repository and Version Control Security
topics.d: Securing source code repositories including access controls, secrets prevention, branch protection, and code signing.

topics.t: Web Application Security Beyond OWASP Top 10
topics.d: Advanced web application security topics including business logic flaws, race conditions, deserialization attacks, and server-side request forgery.
Managing software configurations and changes securely including version control, change advisory boards, and configuration auditing.

Security must be integrated into every phase of the Software Development Life Cycle, not bolted on at the end. Requirements, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance all have security activities.

The OWASP Top 10 represents the most critical web application security risks. Understanding each vulnerability category, attack vectors, and defenses is essential for both the exam and practical security.

topics.t: Secure Coding Practices: Input Validation and Output Encoding
topics.d: Input validation and output encoding are the two most critical secure coding practices. Input validation ensures data meets expectations before processing. Output encoding prevents interpreted injection when displaying data.

Different SDLC models suit different project types. Waterfall is sequential, Agile is iterative, Spiral emphasizes risk analysis, and DevOps integrates development and operations. Each has different security integration points.

topics.t: Database Security: Inference, Aggregation, and Polyinstantiation
topics.d: Databases face unique security challenges. Inference attacks derive classified info from unclassified data. Aggregation combines low-classification data to derive higher-classification conclusions. Polyinstantiation prevents both.

Software supply chain attacks target the development pipeline, third-party components, and distribution mechanisms. The SolarWinds attack demonstrated devastating impact. SBOM, code signing, and dependency scanning are key defenses.

topics.t: API Security and Common API Vulnerabilities
topics.d: APIs are the backbone of modern applications and a growing attack surface. OWASP API Security Top 10 identifies the most critical API risks. Authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and input validation are essential API security controls.

topics.t: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Security
topics.d: AI/ML systems introduce new security challenges including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, model theft, and privacy concerns. Understanding these risks and defenses is increasingly relevant for CISSP.

Buffer overflows occur when a program writes data beyond allocated memory boundaries. Stack-based and heap-based overflows can lead to code execution. Prevention requires secure coding, compiler protections, and OS mitigations.

Containers (Docker, Kubernetes) and serverless platforms introduce new security considerations. Container image security, orchestration hardening, secrets management, and serverless function isolation are key concerns.
HTTP security headers protect against common web attacks. CSP prevents XSS, HSTS enforces HTTPS, X-Frame-Options prevents clickjacking, and other headers harden the browser security context.

Session management maintains user state across HTTP requests. Insecure session handling leads to session hijacking, fixation, and replay attacks. Secure implementation requires random IDs, proper cookie flags, and timeout controls.

Insecure deserialization allows attackers to manipulate serialized objects to execute arbitrary code, tamper with data, or escalate privileges. It is a critical vulnerability in Java, .NET, PHP, and Python applications.

topics.t: Software Composition Analysis and Dependency Management
topics.d: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) identifies open-source and third-party components in applications, checking for known vulnerabilities, license compliance, and outdated dependencies.

Threat modeling systematically identifies potential threats to a system. Methodologies include STRIDE, PASTA, VAST, attack trees, and LINDDUN, each offering different perspectives on threat identification.
Code signing uses digital signatures to verify the authenticity and integrity of software. It ensures code has not been tampered with and comes from a verified publisher.
Runtime protection monitors applications during execution to detect and prevent attacks in real time. Technologies include RASP, WAF, and runtime integrity checking.

Microservices decompose applications into small, independently deployable services. This architecture introduces unique security challenges including service-to-service authentication, API gateway security, and distributed secrets management.
Mobile application security addresses unique challenges of mobile platforms including insecure data storage, insufficient transport security, improper platform usage, and reverse engineering risks.
End-of-life (EOL) software management includes decommissioning applications safely, migrating data, revoking access, and ensuring no orphaned resources remain that could become security liabilities.

topics.t: Privacy by Design in Software Development
topics.d: Privacy by Design (PbD) embeds privacy protections into software from the design phase rather than retrofitting them. Ann Cavoukian's 7 foundational principles guide privacy-aware development.
Secure API design encompasses authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting, and proper error handling. REST, GraphQL, and gRPC each have unique security considerations.

Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defines infrastructure in version-controlled templates. Security scanning of IaC templates catches misconfigurations before deployment, implementing shift-left security for infrastructure.

topics.t: Source Code Management and DevSecOps Pipeline
topics.d: Secure source code management includes access controls, branch protection, code review requirements, and secrets scanning. DevSecOps integrates security testing into every stage of the CI/CD pipeline.
